The ayah comes shortly after the description of hearts settling by remembrance, and it names what those described receive. The commentators note that the promise here is unusually compressed beside the surah's earlier description of the Gardens, and read the two as complementary rather than as alternatives to each other.

keyTerms.note: A form from the root for what is good and pleasant, occurring only here in the Quran. Commentators offer several readings, including a state of gladness, a good end, and a named tree, and they preserve them all.
A noun of place from the verb to come back. It names a destination defined by returning rather than by arriving, so what is promised is somewhere you go back to rather than somewhere new.
From a root meaning to be in good repair, the same one behind the verb for reconciling people. Good deeds are named as things that work properly rather than as things that earn credit.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The word for a place of return had a physical meaning for people who moved seasonally. A tribe left its grazing ground and came back to it, and the coming back was the point of the leaving. Naming a destination that way told listeners that what was promised was not an unfamiliar place but the one they had come from, which is a particular kind of comfort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for what the believers receive occurs only once in the whole Quran. The classical commentators list several readings of it, among them a state of gladness, a good end, and a tree in the Garden so large that a rider could travel a long time in its shade, and they record those readings side by side without ranking them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah promises something without fully specifying it, and the commentators' inability to settle the word is part of how it works on a reader. What is named clearly is the second half, a place of return, and what is left open is the first. That combination gives a definite destination and an indefinite good, which is roughly how the Quran describes what is coming throughout.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same destination at greater length, with who is met there and what is said.
Names the condition of the people this ayah promises, hearts settled by remembrance.
Uses the same word for a place of return, contrasting it with what people are drawn to here.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of what you look forward to is described to you in detail, and how little of it satisfies when it arrives. This ayah promises something and then refuses to specify it. Try, once this week, wanting something you cannot picture. It is a different exercise from planning, and considerably harder.

studies.title: He Is My Lord
studies.meaning: The messenger is placed in a line of others and given a task described by one verb: to recite what has been revealed. Then a fact about the audience, that they deny the Merciful, and then a reply made of four short statements. Each one is personal. He is my Lord; there is no god but He; upon Him I rely; and to Him is my turning back. The reply argues nothing at all. It states a position and stops there.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. The classical sources report that the name used here for God, the Merciful, was objected to by some as an unfamiliar way of addressing Him, and several commentators connect this ayah to that objection. The passage belongs to the surah's closing section, where the messenger's own position is stated rather than defended.

keyTerms.note: From a root connected both with a mother and with intending a direction. It names a group by what it moves towards rather than by descent, which is why the word can cover a nation and a period at once.
An intensive form built on the root for the womb. The classical sources report that some found this an unfamiliar name to use of God, which is precisely what the ayah is answering here.
A noun from the verb behind repentance, with the possessive attached. It closes the sentence with the speaker's own destination rather than with any claim about the people who have just denied him.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Names for God varied across Arabia, and different regions used different ones. A name that was ordinary in one place could sound foreign in another, and objecting to a name was a recognisable way of rejecting the thing named without having to argue about it. That is the situation this ayah reports, and the reply simply uses the name again.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran records this objection to the name directly at 25:60, where people are told to prostrate to the Merciful and answer by asking what the Merciful is. Here the objection is only noted in passing, and the response is not an explanation of the name but a four-part statement about who the speaker takes his Lord to be.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply is entirely in the first person and makes no claim at all about the objectors. Faced with a rejection of a name, the answer is a statement of one's own position, four clauses long, without argument and without reproach. That models a kind of response the surah has not yet demonstrated, and it puts reliance and return at the end, so the last word concerns where the speaker is going.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same objection to the name directly, put in the form of a question.
Answers the same objection about which name to use, and settles it a different way.
Ends another messenger's reply with the same two statements, reliance and turning back.

studies.applyIt: The next time somebody dismisses something you hold, try answering only about yourself. Not a defence and not a counter-argument: one or two sentences saying what you actually rely on. It is a much shorter reply than the one you were preparing, and it ends the exchange without requiring anybody to lose.

studies.title: Even If Mountains Moved
studies.meaning: A conditional sentence deliberately left unfinished. If there were a recitation that moved mountains, split the earth open, or made the dead speak, and then the second half never arrives. Commentators discuss the gap at length and supply it as this would be that recitation. The argument then turns: the whole matter belongs to God, and had He willed, everyone would have been guided. So the missing conclusion is answered by a fact about how belief actually works.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with the commentators recording disagreement. The ayah answers the demand for a sign that this surah has already quoted twice. The three examples given, moving mountains and splitting the earth and speaking to the dead, are extreme cases, and the commentators read them as the largest signs anyone could ask for, named here in order to be set aside.

keyTerms.note: The passive of the verb for making something travel. The Quran uses it elsewhere of mountains on the last day, so the example named here is not fanciful but taken from what has already been promised.
From the verb to knock or strike hard, so the word names a calamity by its sound. It also titles surah 101, where it becomes a name for the last day itself rather than for any ordinary trouble.
A meeting with a place and a time agreed between two parties. The word occurs four times in the Quran, and the sentence it closes here also closes a prayer near the end of surah 3.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed points of the landscape. Routes, boundaries and stories were all keyed to them, and they were the standard image for what does not move. Naming the moving of mountains as a hypothetical sign reached for the least likely event a listener could picture, and the ayah names it in order to say that even that would settle nothing.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this ayah uses for a striking disaster becomes the title of surah 101, where it names the last day. It occurs five times in the Quran and three of those are packed into the opening three ayat of that very short surah. Here alone it is used of an ordinary calamity rather than of the end of everything.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that the largest imaginable sign would not produce belief, and it gives a reason: guiding everybody was always available and was not done. That places belief outside the category of things evidence compels, without saying that evidence is worthless. The ayah then closes on a kept appointment, so the argument ends with a promise rather than with a verdict on anyone.

crossReferences.why: Makes the same claim about signs that are demanded, and lists what would still not suffice.
Quotes the demand for a sign that this ayah finally answers at the surah's close.
Closes a prayer with the same sentence about God keeping the appointment He has made.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself what would actually change your mind about something you already half doubt. Write the answer down. Then ask whether, if it happened, you would in fact change. Most people discover the honest answer is no, which is what this ayah says about signs, without any reproach attached.

studies.title: Mocked Before You Too
studies.meaning: A consolation delivered as a piece of history, and the sequence inside it carries the weight. Messengers before were mocked; those who denied were given a stretch of time; then they were seized. The final clause is a question with no answer supplied, asking how the consequence turned out to be. Commentators note that the word used here for granting time appears elsewhere in the Quran too, always describing an interval that gets mistaken for safety.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. This consolation belongs to the closing section, which returns to the position of the messenger himself after a long stretch of argument. The commentators report no particular occasion, and read the pattern named here as the same one the surah invoked earlier when it spoke of examples that had already passed.

keyTerms.note: A passive form of a verb meaning to make light of something. Mockery is a distinct kind of opposition, since it does not engage a claim but lowers the person carrying it, and the Quran names it separately from denial.
The verb for letting out slack, spoken here in the first person, which is unusual. It occurs in this exact form only twice in the Quran, and both times what follows the interval is a seizure.
From the root for a heel, so what follows wrongdoing is named as the thing coming along behind it. The possessive ending is elided in the Arabic, which gives the closing question its abruptness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mockery was a weapon with professionals attached. Satirical verse was commissioned, memorised and repeated at gatherings, and a well-made line could follow a man for the rest of his life and be recited about his children afterwards. Being laughed at in that setting was not a mild social difficulty. It was a campaign with a known technique and known practitioners.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for granting time occurs in this exact first-person past form only twice in the Quran, here and at 22:44, and in both places what follows immediately is a seizure. The shift into a single speaker for a sentence about respite and consequence is unusual enough that the commentators pause on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The consolation offered here promises neither relief nor vindication. It describes a pattern that has already run, and it ends on a question rather than a claim, which leaves a reader to supply what they already know. That is a particular kind of comfort: not that this will pass, but that its shape is familiar, and that the interval now being taken for safety has been misread before.

crossReferences.why: Names the same pattern earlier in the surah, of examples that had already passed by.
Explains the same interval from the other side, as a lengthening rather than a favour.
States the same consolation and adds what happened to the mockery itself afterwards.

studies.applyIt: If you are being made a joke of somewhere, resist the two obvious moves: answering in kind, and pretending you have not noticed. Do neither for a week. The ayah offers no strategy and no promise about the mockers, only the observation that this has a known shape. Sometimes that alone is enough to stand in.

studies.title: Name Them, Then
studies.meaning: Another unfinished comparison. The One standing over every soul with whatever it has earned, and then the sentence breaks off without completing the contrast. What follows is a challenge in two words: name them. Commentators explain the demand as asking for a description, since anything that could actually be named would need qualities that could be checked. Two alternatives are offered and both are unflattering: informing Him of something on earth He does not know, or a surface of words.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The ayah returns to the challenge put at 13:16 and sharpens it. The commentators note the unfinished construction and read it as the same technique used earlier in the surah, where a comparison is set up and the listener left to complete it. The closing clause connects the refusal to a scheme made attractive to those making it.

keyTerms.note: The participle of the verb to stand, used of somebody overseeing work or holding a post. It describes an attentive presence rather than knowledge alone, and the phrase it forms here occurs only in this ayah.
Two syllables carrying the whole challenge. Naming in Arabic means giving a description that actually fits, so the demand is for an account that could be examined rather than merely for a label.
The first word means outward or apparent, so the phrase describes words with nothing but an exterior. It names talk that has a shape and no content behind it, which is the second alternative offered.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Naming in Arabia was a serious business. A name recorded a quality, an incident or a lineage, and it could be given, earned or lost. Nicknames stuck for generations and were used as arguments in disputes. Demanding that somebody name a thing was asking them to say what it actually was, in front of people who would test the description.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase describing God as standing over every soul with what it has earned occurs only in this ayah, and so does the two-word challenge to name them. The sentence is also grammatically incomplete: the comparison it opens is never finished, and the commentators supply the missing half from the sense of the surrounding passage.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The challenge is about knowledge rather than about polemics. It does not argue that the alternatives are weak; it asks for a description, and then points out that there are only two possibilities if one is supplied, both of which undo the claim. That shows a position to have no content rather than to be mistaken, which is a different kind of refutation and a harder one to answer.

crossReferences.why: Puts the same challenge earlier in the surah, about protectors that cannot help themselves.
Answers the same challenge directly, saying that only the names themselves exist.
Uses the identical question about informing God of something, in almost the same words.

studies.applyIt: Take something you say you believe and try to state it in one sentence that could be checked. Not a slogan and not a feeling. If you cannot, that is worth knowing, and it is not a verdict on the belief. The ayah's demand is simply that a claim have a shape somebody could examine.

studies.title: No Defender Against Him
studies.meaning: A short ayah in three clauses, moving from the present to what follows and then to a denial. There is something painful in this nearer life; what comes after it is harder; and there is nobody to shield them from it. The word for harder is unusual, meaning more difficult to bear rather than more acute. Commentators discuss what the present suffering refers to and record several readings, from defeat and loss to the condition of a person who has closed their own hearing.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. The ayah follows the challenge to name what has been set up beside God and completes it. Its closing word, for a defender or shield, appears again three ayat later applied to the messenger himself, so the same protection is denied to two very different people within a few lines.

keyTerms.note: A comparative from the root for splitting, used of hardship rather than of pain. What is described is a weight harder to carry rather than a sensation more acute, which is a deliberate distinction.
The participle from the verb to guard against something, the same root behind the word for mindfulness of God. It occurs twice in this surah and once elsewhere, and always inside a denial.

The adjective is a comparative meaning closer, not lower. Arabic names this life by its proximity rather than by any judgement on its quality, which the usual translation as worldly slightly obscures.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Protection in Arabia was a named relationship you could point at. If you were threatened, somebody stood between you and the threat, and everyone knew who that was for each person in a settlement. Saying a man had no shield at all described a condition people could picture exactly, and it was the most exposed position anybody in that society could hold.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a shield used at the end of this ayah appears again three ayat later at 13:37, where it is applied to the messenger himself inside a conditional sentence. Within a few lines the same protection is denied to two entirely different people, once as a consequence and once as a warning about what would follow.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah refuses to postpone everything to a later date. Something is happening already, and the classical readings of what that is are varied enough to suggest it is not one obvious event. The comparative is then chosen carefully: what comes is harder rather than sharper. And the closing clause removes the option people reach for first, which is not escape but rescue by somebody stronger.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a shield, applied there to the messenger in a conditional warning.
Uses the identical phrase about having no defender against God, of earlier peoples.
Sets the same comparison between this life and the next, measured a different way.

studies.applyIt: Notice who you assume will step in if something goes badly wrong: a parent, an employer, a savings account, a person with influence. Name them honestly. Then hold the ayah's last clause beside that list, not as a threat but as a question about how much weight each of those names can actually take.

studies.title: Its Food And Its Shade
studies.meaning: A description made almost entirely of one repeated word: perpetual. The rivers run beneath, and then two things are named as unending, food and shade. Commentators note the choice, since these are not gold or company or peace but the two things a desert traveller runs out of. The closing sentence then names the other outcome in four words, so a description of one destination is balanced against a very short statement about its opposite.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with the commentators recording disagreement about it. The word opening the description means a likeness or comparison, which the commentators take seriously: what follows is presented as an approximation rather than a report. The same opening phrase occurs once more in the Quran, at 47:15, where the description after it is considerably longer.

keyTerms.note: The word for a parable or similitude. Its presence at the head of the description signals an approximation rather than a report, which the commentators take seriously when reading everything that follows it.
From a verb meaning to go on without interruption. It is applied to the food and to the shade together, and what it denies is not scarcity but the ending that everything in this world eventually has.
From the root for a heel, so the word names what comes along behind. This surah uses it three times, which makes it one of the chapter's own characteristic terms for a final result.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Shade in Arabia was a resource rather than a comfort. Travellers timed a day's stage by where shade would fall at noon, and a tree at a known point on a route was a landmark with a name. Food and shade were the two things that ran out on a journey and the two a host supplied on arrival. Naming those as perpetual answered the anxiety of the road.
studies.didYouKnow: The opening phrase of this ayah, naming the likeness of the Garden promised to the mindful, occurs twice in the Quran. Here it introduces a description two lines long; at 47:15 the identical phrase opens a description several times longer. One formula serves both a compressed account and an expanded one.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The description is deliberately modest, and that modesty is itself a claim. What is promised is named in the vocabulary of relief from ordinary hardship rather than in the vocabulary of splendour. And the word standing at the head of the sentence concedes that this is a comparison, so a reader is given something they can picture while being told plainly that the picture is not the thing.

crossReferences.why: Opens with the identical phrase and gives a much longer description of the same place.
Describes the same destination earlier in the surah, naming company rather than provisions.
Extends the same imagery of shade and unfailing fruit at considerably greater length.

studies.applyIt: Notice what you actually run out of, rather than what you would like more of. Sleep, patience, quiet, money at the end of the month. The two things named here are the two that ran out on a desert road. Name yours honestly this week; it tells you what a promise of perpetual would mean to you.

studies.title: I Am Commanded To Worship
studies.meaning: Two reactions are reported side by side and neither is explained. Some of those given the earlier scripture rejoice at what has been revealed; among the factions, some refuse to recognise part of it. The reply that follows addresses neither group. It states the speaker's own instruction in four clauses, naming worship, the refusal to associate anything, an invitation, and a return. Commentators note that the reply narrows the ground rather than arguing over it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The word rendered as parties or factions is used across the Quran for coalitions of opponents, and the commentators read it here as covering groups from more than one community. The reply follows the pattern set a few ayat earlier at 13:30, where an objection is met with a first-person statement rather than a rebuttal.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a group bound by a common cause, used across the Quran of coalitions formed against a messenger. It names people by their alignment rather than by any belief they hold.
The verb for denying that you know something, the opposite of acknowledging it. What is described is a refusal to recognise part of what is presented, rather than an argument against the whole.
The verb for calling somebody towards you, the same one used for prayer. The speaker's task is named with a word that faces outward, and it is followed straight away by the word for his own return.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina held communities with older scriptures and long-established scholarship, and reactions to a new claim were never uniform inside any of them. Individuals crossed over, argued, or accepted parts and refused others, and all of it happened in public. Reporting two responses in one sentence describes a city where nobody could speak for a whole community.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for factions used here occurs ten times in the Quran and is nearly always applied to coalitions formed against a messenger rather than to any settled community. It names a group by what it has assembled against, which is why this ayah can use it of people drawn from more than one background at the same time.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply answers a divided reception with an undivided statement. Rather than sorting the objectors, it restates what the speaker was instructed to do, and every clause of it is in the first person. That refusal to negotiate over parts does something specific: a message accepted in fragments is treated as a different thing from the message, and nobody is condemned for the fragments they took.

crossReferences.why: Answers a different objection with the same technique, a first-person statement rather than a rebuttal.
Names the same partial reception directly, and puts it to the reader as a question.
Reports the same positive reception among people holding an earlier scripture.

studies.applyIt: Think about which parts of what you believe you actually act on and which you have quietly filed away. Everyone does this and it is rarely deliberate. Pick one filed item and take it out this week. The ayah does not attack anyone for it; it simply states what the whole instruction was.

studies.title: Sent Down In Arabic
studies.meaning: The revelation is described in two words, a judgement and Arabic, which the commentators unpack as decisive guidance delivered in a particular language. Then a conditional aimed at the messenger himself: were you to follow their leanings after the knowledge that has reached you, you would have neither ally nor shield. Commentators note the severity of addressing this to him, and read it as establishing that the message is not his property to adjust.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. The phrase naming the revelation as an Arabic judgement occurs only here. The conditional that follows belongs to a group of passages addressed to the messenger in the same form, warning against accommodation, which the commentators read as instructive for the audience rather than as suggesting any likelihood.

keyTerms.note: From the root for restraining and deciding, which also gives the words for wisdom and for a bridle. What it names is guidance that settles matters, so the noun carries the sense of ending disputes rather than starting them.

The adjective names the language, and its pairing with a word for judgement occurs only in this ayah. The Quran repeatedly notes the language of its own delivery, treating that as part of what is being described.

From a root meaning to fall or incline, the same one behind the word for air. Desires are pictured as a slope you slide down rather than as choices, which is why following them is described as a direction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabic was a prestige language for its own speakers and a marginal one beyond them, with Persian, Greek and Syriac carrying the empires and the older scriptures around Arabia. Naming a revelation as Arabic was therefore a claim about a language people had heard dismissed, and about an audience that had not previously received a scripture in its own speech.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact phrase naming this revelation as an Arabic judgement occurs only in this ayah. The Quran refers to the language of its own delivery a number of times elsewhere, always in the same way, as a fact about how the message arrives rather than as a claim that the language itself is superior to any other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Addressing the warning to the messenger does something structural. If the person delivering a message would have no protection for adjusting it, then the message is clearly not his to adjust, and everybody listening learns that in the strongest available form. The pairing of judgement with language also says something modest: what settles matters arrives in a particular tongue, at a particular time, to particular people.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for a shield three ayat earlier, applied to a very different group.
Gives the same conditional warning to the messenger about following their desires.
Names the language of the revelation and gives a reason for it directly.

studies.applyIt: Notice where you soften something true because of who is listening. Not tact, which is a courtesy, but the version that removes what the other person would dislike. Pick one such conversation this week and say the unsoftened sentence kindly. The difficulty of doing it is what this ayah is describing.

studies.title: He Erases And Confirms
studies.meaning: Three statements about messengers, then one about writing. Earlier messengers had spouses and children, which answers an objection without stating it. No messenger produced a sign except by permission, so the power was never theirs. Every term has a writing. Then the second ayah: God erases what He wills and fixes what He wills, and with Him is the source of the Book. Commentators differ widely over what is erased, and record the range rather than settling it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with the commentators recording disagreement about it. The first statement answers a recorded objection that a man with a household could not be a messenger, which appears elsewhere in the Quran in similar terms. The second ayah has attracted extensive classical discussion, with readings ranging from records of deeds to instructions later replaced to the terms of a lifespan.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word meaning one of a pair. Naming it of earlier messengers answers an assumption that a prophet must stand outside ordinary life, and it does so by reporting rather than by arguing.
The verb for rubbing something off a surface, used of writing removed from a tablet. It assumes a written medium, which is why the phrase closing the ayah names a book rather than a decision.
The Arabic says the mother of the Book, and the word for a mother is used in Arabic for an origin or a principal thing. So the phrase names a master copy rather than any maternal relation.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Writing in that world was on materials made to be reused. Wooden boards were whitewashed, written on and washed clean again; leather and parchment were scraped and used a second time. Erasing and fixing were two ordinary stages of one craft, and any scribe would have heard the pair as a description of work in progress rather than of indecision.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing the second ayah, naming the source of the Book, occurs three times in the Quran: here, at 3:7 and at 43:4. In each place it stands at the end of a passage about what is fixed and what is open to interpretation, and in each place it names something held with God rather than in anybody's hands.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The two ayat together do something careful. The first insists that messengers were ordinary and dependent, with households and with no power over signs. The second places all the deciding elsewhere, in a book that is written and edited. Between them, everything that might be credited to the person delivering a message is moved away from him, which is what this surah has been doing since its opening line.

crossReferences.why: Records the objection this ayah answers, that a messenger should not live an ordinary life.
Uses the same phrase for the source of the Book, in a passage about clear and unclear ayat.
Makes the same point about signs, that the whole matter belongs to God alone.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much you expect of people you admire, and how quickly ordinariness in them reads as disqualification. The first sentence here names households and children as facts about prophets. Give one person you look up to permission this week to be tired, wrong, or busy with something small.

studies.title: Yours To Tell, Ours To Reckon
studies.meaning: A sentence built as a division of labour. Whether you are shown some of what We promise them, or We take you first, the two tasks are then named: yours is the delivering, ours is the reckoning. The conditional is unusual because both branches lead to the same conclusion, so nothing turns on which of them happens. Commentators note the two possessives, which carry the whole meaning: two jobs assigned, and only one of them to the person addressed.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded. The ayah belongs to a group of passages addressing the messenger about outcomes he might not live to see, and the commentators read it as answering an unspoken concern rather than a stated objection. Similar sentences appear in several surahs, always separating the task of conveying from the task of judging.

keyTerms.note: A causative of the verb to see, carrying an emphatic ending. The first branch of the conditional is about witnessing rather than about achieving, so what he might or might not be given is a sight.

The verb for collecting a payment completely, used across the Quran for death. Placing it as the alternative to seeing an outcome treats dying as simply the other branch, with no extra weight attached.
From the verb to reach a destination, so the noun names getting a message all the way to its recipient. It says nothing about what happens after arrival, which is the entire point of the division.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger in Arabia carried words and was not answerable for them. He crossed to another tribe, delivered what he had been given, and returned, and what the recipients did about it lay between them and whoever had sent him. The role was well defined and well understood, and this ayah uses its exact vocabulary to describe a much larger commission.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase saying that only the conveying is upon you occurs three times in the Quran, here and at 3:20 and 16:82. Each time it closes an exchange rather than opening one, and each time the sentence around it makes the same division: delivery on one side, and everything that follows delivery on the other.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah releases a person from responsibility for a result, and it does so in the middle of a passage about opponents who have not been persuaded. That is a specific consolation and also a specific limit. It treats the two possible futures as equivalent, which quietly says that seeing the outcome of your work was never part of the assignment.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same phrase about the duty being only to convey, at the close of an argument.
Gives almost the same conditional about being shown some of it or being taken first.
Names the same office earlier in the surah, describing the messenger as only a warner.

studies.applyIt: Pick one thing you are carrying that is not actually yours to settle: someone else's decision, a change at work, how a relative treats you. Write out, in two short lines, what your part is and what is not your part. Then do only your part this week and notice how much room that leaves.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: Reduced At Its Edges
studies.meaning: A question about something visible, and the image is territorial: We come to the land and reduce it from its outer parts. Commentators divide over what is meant, reading it as territory lost by opponents, as the death of scholars and notable people, or as the physical wearing of the earth. Then two short clauses close it. God judges, and nothing comes behind His judgement to reverse it. The final phrase names the speed of the reckoning.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. The same wording occurs once more in the Quran, at 21:44, in a similar setting. The commentators note that the ayah asks whether people have seen something, which implies a process already visible at the time, and their differing readings reflect real uncertainty about what the first listeners were being pointed towards.

keyTerms.note: The verb for making something less, used of measures and of numbers. It describes subtraction rather than destruction, so what is named is a steady diminishing rather than any single catastrophe.
The plural of a word for a limb or an outer point. It can mean the borders of a territory or the ends of a thing, and the commentators' disagreement largely turns on which sense is intended.
From the root for a heel, so the word names somebody coming along behind to overturn what was done. It belongs to the language of judgement, where an appeal follows a decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Land in Arabia was held at its margins. Grazing rights, wells and control of routes were contested at the edges of a tribe's range, and a territory shrank by losing its outer places one at a time rather than by being taken whole. Anybody who moved animals seasonally understood a range diminishing from the rim inwards, because they had watched it happen.
studies.didYouKnow: This sentence appears twice in the Quran, here and at 21:44, in nearly identical words, and both times as a question about something people should already have noticed. The classical commentators offer several readings of what is being diminished and record them all rather than choosing, which is unusual for a phrase repeated so exactly.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah points at a process rather than an event and asks whether it has been noticed. That is a different kind of evidence from a sign: gradual, already under way, and easy to live inside without registering at all. The closing clauses then say that this is judgement in progress and that nothing follows it to overturn it, which makes the gradual thing the serious one.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same sentence in almost identical words, inside a similar warning.
Names the same kind of ongoing calamity earlier in the surah, striking near their homes.
States the same claim that judgement belongs to God and to nobody called upon beside Him.

studies.applyIt: Think about what has been shrinking in your life at the edges rather than collapsing in the middle: energy, a friendship group, the number of hours you get to yourself. Nothing has gone wrong, so nothing has demanded attention. Name one such edge today and decide whether you mind. That is the ayah's question, in miniature.

studies.title: The Whole Plan Is His
studies.meaning: A short ayah with a large reversal in it. Those before them planned, and then the sentence takes the word back: the entire planning belongs to God. Commentators note the construction, which does not say that His plan is better but that all of it is His, and that is a stronger claim. Then a statement about knowing what every soul earns, and a closing promise that those who deny will find out whose the final outcome is.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with the commentators recording disagreement. The ayah belongs to the last few lines of the chapter, which gather several of its threads together: the pattern of earlier peoples, the knowledge of what is hidden, and the final outcome. The word for outcome used at the end appears three times in this surah, which commentators note as one of its characteristic terms.

keyTerms.note: The verb for arranging something the other party cannot see. It is used first of people and then of God inside one sentence, which the commentators explain as answering a hidden plan in kind rather than as deception.
One word that turns the sentence from a comparison into a claim about ownership. It does not say His planning is better; it says the whole category is His, which leaves nothing standing outside it.
An idiom for the final result, built on the word for what follows behind. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah, which makes it one of its own expressions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Planning was often the only weapon a smaller party had. An ambush at a well, a false report sent ahead, an alliance arranged quietly before a dispute broke: these decided outcomes more often than numbers did. Everyone understood that the invisible half of a conflict mattered most, which is why a claim about who owns the planning would have landed hard.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the final outcome used at the end of this ayah occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah, at 13:22, 13:24 and here. The first two describe what the patient receive. This one leaves the question open and says that those who deny will find out for themselves.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reversal in the first line is the whole ayah. Saying that all planning belongs to God is not a claim that His scheme will beat other schemes, which would leave the others real and merely weaker. It says the category itself is His, so a hidden plan is not a second thing running alongside. The clause about knowledge then closes the gap from the other side.

crossReferences.why: Describes a specific plot answered in kind, using the same verb of both parties.
States the same principle at its largest scale, that no scheme escapes the reckoning.
Uses the same phrase for the final outcome, applied there to those who were patient.

studies.applyIt: Think of a situation where you suspect something is being arranged without you. The ayah does not tell you what it is or promise you a good result. It says the category of hidden arranging is not a place where you are alone. Act on what you can see this week, and stop rehearsing what you cannot.

studies.title: God Is Witness Enough
studies.meaning: The surah closes on the flattest possible denial, that he is not a messenger at all, and on a reply that calls witnesses. The first is God, described as sufficient, which settles the matter on its own. Then a second is added, whoever has knowledge of the Book, and the commentators divide over who that names: God under another description, people holding earlier scripture, or those who know the revelation being given. The surah ends without resolving it.
studies.historicalContext: The surah is classified as Medinan, with disagreement recorded among the commentators. The denial reported here is the simplest form of the objection the surah has been answering since its opening ayah, and the reply is correspondingly short. The disagreement over the second witness is an old one, and the classical commentaries set the readings out side by side without preferring any of them.

keyTerms.note: The verb for something being adequate to a need, with no comparison implied. Its use here means the testimony closes the matter, rather than that it outweighs whatever the other side might bring forward.
From the verb for being present and seeing. Arabic builds testimony out of presence, so a witness is somebody who was there, which is why the same word can also name one who dies for a cause.
The phrase occurs only in this ayah. Its indeterminacy is exactly why the commentators divide over it, and the surah closes on a description rather than on any name.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Testimony was the entire legal system. There were no records, so a claim stood or fell on who would appear and say what they had seen, and the standing of a witness mattered as much as their words. Naming a witness was the ordinary way of closing an argument, and everybody in the audience knew exactly what the move meant.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase naming the second witness, whoever has knowledge of the Book, occurs only in this ayah in the whole Quran. The classical commentators record several readings of it and do not settle the question, so the surah closes on a description that has never been finally identified with any one party.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The reply answers a denial of office with an appeal to testimony rather than to proof, which fits this surah's whole approach. It has spent forty ayat pointing at things a person can already see and declining to produce the sign that was demanded. Ending on a witness rather than on a demonstration is consistent with that, and the closing ambiguity leaves a reader still looking.

crossReferences.why: Opens the surah with the claim this denial answers, that the revelation is the truth.
Uses the same formula about God being sufficient as a witness between two parties.
Adds the testimony of the angels to God's own, in a similar reply to the same denial.

studies.applyIt: Notice how much of your energy goes into being believed by people who have already decided. The reply here is one sentence long and names a witness rather than making a case. Pick one argument you keep re-fighting and stop making the case in it. Say what is true once, and let it stand.
